name: World Trade Center Aluminium on Mars
short_status: Still on Mars: aluminium from the World Trade Center site, machined into the rock abrasion tool cable shield on each of Spirit and Opportunity, rovers that fell silent in March 2010 and June 2018.
page_title: World Trade Center Aluminium on Mars
tagline: Honeybee Robotics, with NASA JPL · United States · Artefact · 2004 · The long occupation Success
stats: cable shields, one on Spirit's rock abrasion tool and one on Opportunity's
the day the aluminium reached Honeybee Robotics from the New York mayor's office
when the origin of the metal was first discussed publicly, ten months after the rovers landed

facts.label: What the object is
facts.value: An aluminium cuff that serves as the cable shield, also called the cable guard, on the rock abrasion tool of each Mars Exploration Rover. The tool needed that part anyway; it was not added for the memorial. The metal bears an image of an American flag.

facts.label: Where the metal came from
facts.value: Aluminium recovered from the destroyed World Trade Center towers in the weeks after their destruction. Through contacts of Honeybee Robotics chairman Stephen Gorevan, a parcel was delivered to the company from the New York mayor's office on 1 December 2001. Inside was a twisted plate of aluminium and a note reading "Here is debris from Tower 1 and Tower 2."

facts.label: Whose idea it was
facts.value: Steve Kondos, then a JPL engineer working closely with the Honeybee team, suggested including something on the rovers as an interplanetary memorial. JPL was building the rovers and managing the project.

facts.label: Who made it
facts.value: Tom Myrick, an engineer at Honeybee, saw that the aluminium could be machined into the cable shields. He hand-carried the material to the machine shop in Round Rock, Texas that was already making other parts of the tools, and when the shields came back to New York he affixed an image of the American flag to each one. The work involved Honeybee Robotics, the New York mayor's office, the Texas shop, JPL, and the rover missions' science leader Steve Squyres at Cornell.

facts.label: Where the company was
facts.value: Honeybee Robotics occupied a building on Elizabeth Street in lower Manhattan, less than a mile from the World Trade Center. Normal work stopped for days after the attacks and the smell from the collapse persisted for weeks. On the morning of 11 September 2001 Gorevan was six blocks from the towers, riding his bicycle to work.

facts.label: Why they could not do more
facts.value: JPL's account is specific about the constraint. The rock abrasion tools were on a schedule fixed by the motions of the planets and needed thorough testing before launch, so the people building them could not spend much time helping at shelters or elsewhere. The shields were what they could do.

facts.label: The tool it is part of
facts.value: The rock abrasion tool, built by Honeybee Robotics, is about 7 cm in diameter and 10 cm long, weighs 0.685 kg and draws about 30 W. A diamond-dust wheel turning at about 3,000 rpm grinds a hole 45 mm across and up to 5 mm deep into a rock face, and two brushes sweep the cuttings away so the rover's spectrometers and microscope can look at unweathered material. These figures come from English Wikipedia's article on the tool rather than from a NASA source.

facts.label: First use
facts.value: Spirit first used its rock abrasion tool on 6 February 2004 on a rock the team called Adirondack, grinding about 2.85 mm deep over roughly three hours. Every grind either rover made afterwards was done with this cuff in place on the cable.

facts.label: The first picture
facts.value: Spirit's panoramic camera photographed the shield on 2 February 2004, sol 30 of its mission. NASA published the image as PIA05221 under the title Interplanetary Memorial to Victims of Sept. 11, 2001, noting that an identical piece is on Opportunity.

facts.label: The anniversary picture
facts.value: On 11 September 2011, the tenth anniversary of the attacks, Opportunity photographed its own shield on sol 2,713 using its navigation camera and panoramic camera together. NASA published the combined view as PIA14750.

facts.label: The silence, and the end of it
facts.value: Nobody on the rover team or at Honeybee spoke publicly about the source of the aluminium until late 2004. JPL's account records Gorevan telling a New York Times reporter, for a story published in November 2004 about Manhattan's part in the rover missions, that it had been meant as a quiet tribute, that enough time had passed, and that they wanted the families to know.

facts.label: What Gorevan said about it
facts.value: In JPL's 2011 release Gorevan is quoted as saying it is gratifying to know a piece of the World Trade Center is on Mars, and that the shield contrasts the destructive nature of the attackers with the ingenuity and hopeful attitude of Americans.

facts.label: Where the two shields are now
facts.value: Each shield is on the arm of the rover it was fitted to. Spirit's last downlink reached Earth on 22 March 2010 and NASA ended recovery efforts on 25 May 2011; the rover is at a place called Troy on the west side of the Home Plate plateau in Gusev crater. Opportunity's last transmission reached Earth on 10 June 2018 and NASA declared that mission complete on 13 February 2019; the rover is in Perseverance Valley on the western rim of Endeavour crater. Neither position has a published fix better than the centre of the HiRISE frame that shows the rover.

facts.label: How long they will last
facts.value: JPL's own estimate, published in 2011, is that in the cold, dry environments where the rovers worked the memorials could remain in good condition for millions of years.

facts.label: Not the only 9/11 material on the rovers
facts.value: JPL's 2020 summary of commemorative objects on Mars rovers describes the World Trade Center metal on Spirit and Opportunity in the same paragraph as the Columbia crew memorial carried by Spirit, the Pioneer plaques and the Voyager Golden Records, and calls the practice festooning.

timeline: Honeybee Robotics, on Elizabeth Street in lower Manhattan, is building a pair of rock abrasion tools for NASA's two Mars Exploration Rovers when the World Trade Center, less than a mile away, is destroyed.

Steve Kondos, a JPL engineer working with the Honeybee team, proposes that the rovers carry an interplanetary memorial. The problem becomes how to obtain a suitable piece of material from the site. JPL's account does not date the suggestion; it only places it before the material arrived on 1 December.
A parcel from the New York mayor's office reaches Honeybee Robotics. It contains a twisted plate of aluminium and a note: "Here is debris from Tower 1 and Tower 2."

Between the parcel arriving and the launches, Tom Myrick hand-carries the aluminium to the machine shop in Round Rock, Texas that is making other parts of the tools, and fits an image of the American flag to each finished shield back in New York. JPL's account gives no dates for these steps.
Spirit and Opportunity launch from Cape Canaveral, each with one of the shields on the cable of its rock abrasion tool.
On sol 30 Spirit's panoramic camera photographs the flag on its own tool. NASA publishes the image as PIA05221, Interplanetary Memorial to Victims of Sept. 11, 2001.
Spirit makes the first grind of the mission, into a rock called Adirondack, cutting about 2.85 mm deep in roughly three hours.

A New York Times story about Manhattan's part in the rover missions carries the first public account of where the metal came from. Gorevan tells the reporter it had been meant as a quiet tribute, that enough time has passed, and that they want the families to know.
Spirit's last downlink reaches Earth, from Troy on the west side of Home Plate in Gusev crater. NASA concludes recovery efforts on 25 May 2011. One shield stops moving.

On the tenth anniversary of the attacks, Opportunity photographs its own shield on sol 2,713, combining navigation camera and panoramic camera exposures. NASA publishes the result as PIA14750 the following day.

Opportunity's last transmission reaches Earth from Perseverance Valley as a planet-encircling dust storm blacks out its arrays. NASA declares the mission complete on 13 February 2019. The second shield stops moving.

images.caption: A Spirit panoramic camera image taken on 2 February 2004, sol 30, showing the rover's arm turret against the ground of Gusev crater, with the cylindrical cable guard of the rock abrasion tool at the upper left carrying an image of the United States flag. The shield was machined from aluminium recovered from the World Trade Center site.

A combined view taken by Opportunity on 11 September 2011, sol 2,713, in which a colour panoramic camera frame of the rover's arm turret is inset into a wider grey navigation camera frame of the ground. The flag on the rock abrasion tool's cable guard is at the centre of the colour inset.

A close view of the rock abrasion tool on a full-scale Mars Exploration Rover display model at the Virginia Air and Space Center, photographed in July 2010, with the grinding head, the brush and the flag-marked cylindrical cable guard all visible at arm's length against a simulated Martian floor.
